problem.title: WatchLog found this by itself.
problem.body: Nobody wrote a rule or built a dashboard for it. The default alerts were on from the first minute after one install command.

why.title: The why, in one sentence.
why.kubernetes: WatchLog followed the symptom through the workloads it touches to where it starts. You didn't write a query or open three dashboards.
why.server: WatchLog followed the symptom on the server to where it starts: the service, its last change, its limits. You didn't open a log or ssh in.
why.small: Fixed rules over data the agent already collects. No AI guess, and it says so when it isn't sure.

proof.title: You don't have to take its word for it.
proof.kubernetes: The moment it started is marked on the alert's own chart, and What changed lists what moved around it. Both were there before you asked.
proof.server: The moment it started is marked on the alert's own chart, beside the change that came just before. Both were there before you asked.
proof.next: Get this on my own systems

end.title: A problem, its cause and the proof. Nobody set anything up.

rabbitmq-payments.title: A queue nobody reads
rabbitmq-payments.why: WatchLog followed the queue to its consumer, and the consumer to its memory limit. You didn't write a query or open three dashboards.
rabbitmq-payments.proof: The moment the worker died is marked on the queue's own chart, and the cause names which client stopped reading. Both were there before you asked.

postgres-lock.title: A row held in an idle transaction
postgres-lock.why: WatchLog followed the waiting sessions to the one holding the lock, and to the service whose transaction sits idle. You didn't run a query on the database.
postgres-lock.proof: The moment the lock was taken is marked on the alert's own chart. It was there before you asked.

legacy-importer.title: A container that never starts
legacy-importer.why: WatchLog read how the container ends each time and what changed before it began. You didn't open a log or a terminal.
legacy-importer.proof: Every restart is on the alert's own chart, and the cause says how the container exits. Both were there before you asked.

orders-release.title: A server after a bad release
orders-release.why: WatchLog saw a new orders binary on the server just before the crashes began. You didn't open a log or ssh in.
orders-release.proof: The release is marked on the alert's own chart, right before the first crash. It was there before you asked.

invoices.title: A service that fails since its last change
invoices.why: WatchLog saw a new invoices build on the server just before it started failing. You didn't open a log or ssh in.
invoices.proof: The new build is marked on the alert's own chart, and the service is still failing after it. It was there before you asked.

report-builder.title: A job that fails quietly
report-builder.why: WatchLog can't prove one cause here, so it lists what could explain it and what it checked. It says so when it isn't sure.
report-builder.proof: Every failed run is on the alert's own chart. It was there before you asked.

reasons.setting_risky: {name} is set in a way that risks your data or slows the server.
reasons.pending_restart: {n} changed settings wait for a restart to take effect.
reasons.connections_vs_memory: max_connections ({max}) could need {need} of memory with work_mem, more than twice the {mem} the server may use.
reasons.connection_leak: {who} keeps {n} connections that have all been idle for {idle} or more: probably a connection leak. Connections are at {pct}% of the limit.
reasons.history_list_long: InnoDB's history list is long ({n}): an old transaction keeps purge from cleaning up.
reasons.binlog_fills_disk: The binary logs fill the data volume in {eta} at their last hour's growth.
reasons.buffer_pool_vs_memory: innodb_buffer_pool_size ({pool}) is close to the memory the server may use ({mem}).
reasons.redo_nearly_full: The redo log is {pct}% full: writes stall when the checkpoint can't keep up.
reasons.collscan_fills_cache: Collection scans on {ns}, sent by {client}, fill the cache: {perMin} slow ones a minute, each reading about {examined} documents, and the WiredTiger cache is at {cachePct}%. An index on the fields it filters by would stop them.
reasons.access_control_off: Access control is off: WatchLog connected without a user, and so can anyone who reaches the port.
reasons.backlog_short: The replication backlog ({size}) holds about {seconds} s of writes: a replica disconnected longer than that needs a full resync.
reasons.client_buffer_near_limit: {client} has an output buffer at {pct}% of its {class} limit: Redis disconnects it when the limit is reached.
reasons.cluster_unhealthy: The cluster is not healthy: {failing} slots are failing or unreachable, and keys in them can’t be read or written.
reasons.cursors_no_timeout: {n} cursors that never time out are idle (on {ns}, idle {idle}): each keeps its resources until the client closes it.
reasons.fcv_behind: The feature compatibility version is {fcv} on {version}: the new version’s features stay off until it is raised.
reasons.indexes_unused: {n} indexes have not been used since the server started (largest: {index} on {ns}): each slows every write and takes cache.
reasons.main_thread_saturated: The main thread is saturated ({pct}% of one core): Redis is at its limit whatever the memory says. The costliest command in the slow log is {cmd}, sent by {client}.
reasons.mongos_only: This is a mongos: WatchLog sees its own operations and connections, not the shards’. Add each shard’s replica set as its own service.
reasons.no_password: Redis needs no password and listens on {bind}: anyone who reaches the port can read and change every key.
reasons.no_persistence_store: Nothing is saved to disk (no RDB, no AOF) and most keys have no TTL: a restart loses all {keys} keys ({size}).
reasons.noeviction_cache: The policy is noeviction although {pct}% of the keys have a TTL, as in a cache: when memory is full, writes fail instead of old keys being evicted.
reasons.overcommit_off: vm.overcommit_memory is 0 on this host: a save’s fork can fail when memory is short.
reasons.prefix_fills_memory: Memory is at {memPct}% of maxmemory and keys are being evicted ({evictPerMin} a minute, policy {policy}): keys under {prefix} grew from {from}% to {pct}% of memory in two hours, and {noTtl}% of them have no TTL.
reasons.save_wont_fit: The next save may be killed for memory: its fork needs about {need} of copy-on-write and {left} is left under the memory limit.
reasons.single_member_set: The replica set {set} has a single member: there is no failover if it stops.
reasons.stream_group_orphaned: Group {group} on {stream} is falling behind ({lag} entries): its consumer {consumer} has read nothing for {idle}.
reasons.thp_always: Transparent huge pages are set to always on this host: Redis forks and frees memory more slowly.
reasons.voting_members_even: The replica set has {n} voting members: an even number can split in two with no majority. Make it odd.
reasons.prefix_holds_memory: Memory is at {memPct}% of maxmemory and keys are being evicted ({evictPerMin} a minute, policy {policy}): keys under {prefix} hold {pct}% of memory, and {noTtl}% of them have no TTL.

app.t: A few lines with the Prometheus library for your language: one counter on port 9400.
app.then: Then give the address above: localhost:9400/metrics.

exporter.t: A small program that publishes numbers for something else: a GPU, a queue, a device. WatchLog already collects each server's and container's CPU, memory, disk and network, so node_exporter and cAdvisor aren't needed.

prometheus.who: Only if you already run Prometheus. It keeps scraping as before, and also sends WatchLog the metrics you name.
prometheus.code: Add to prometheus.yml, then reload it
prometheus.keep: The keep rule is what makes it a few metrics and not all of them: name yours in its regex.
prometheus.tied: Series are tied to a workload by their namespace and pod labels, to a server by instance or host.

next.title: What happens next
push: The value arrives within seconds, and this page says so.
It appears under Your metrics, on the server or workload you chose.
Put it on a dashboard, pin it to that page, or alert on it.
scrape: Test the address: WatchLog says what it found, in words.
Scrape it: its metrics appear within a minute.
Pin the ones you care about; the rest stay in the list.
prometheus: Reload Prometheus; samples arrive within a minute.
WatchLog ties them to the servers and workloads it knows.
Only the metrics your keep rule names are sent.

limits.title: Kept under control
limits.series: A series is one line on a chart: one metric with one set of labels. orders_total is 1 series however often you send it. orders_total split by 3 payment methods is 3. There is no limit on how many times you send.
limits.source: One scraped endpoint, or one token's pushes, brings at most {max} series.
limits.remoteWrite: A token's remote write has no cap of its own: a whole Prometheus fits, up to your plan's series.
limits.sources: {max} sources on your plan; {used} in use.
limits.labels: A label with more than 100 values on one metric (ids, emails, paths) gets that metric refused, with the label's name.
limits.full: When the series are all in use, new ones are refused and known ones keep flowing.

stuck.title: Stuck?
stuck.codes: 401: the token isn't whole. 400: the answer names the field. 429: too many calls a second.
stuck.docs: Your first metric in two minutes

tokens.title: Tokens
tokens.about: A token can only send your own metrics and change events to this cluster or fleet. It can't read anything.
tokens.name: Name
tokens.once: Token "{name}": copy it now. It won't be shown again.
tokens.revokeBody: Whatever sends with it stops being stored at once. What it sent stays until it ages out.

find.about: Tries /metrics on the ports WatchLog already sees. Nothing restarts.
find.nothingToTry: Nothing to try: WatchLog sees no listening port here that could have a /metrics page.
find.noAnswer: No answer from the collector yet. It may be an older version: update the agent and try again.
find.found: 1 endpoint with metrics, of {asked} tried. | {n} endpoints with metrics, of {asked} tried.
find.triedServer: Tried /metrics on 1 listening port: {ports}. | Tried /metrics on {n} listening ports: {ports}.
find.triedKube: Tried /metrics on 1 port of {workloads}: {ports}. | Tried /metrics on {n} ports of {workloads}: {ports}.
find.skipped: Left out {ports}: they speak their own protocol (SSH, a database), never metrics.
find.scraped: 1 port is scraped already. | {n} ports are scraped already.

sources.title: Sources

dropped.sources: Over your plan's {max} sources: nothing of it is stored. Remove a source, or upgrade.
dropped.sourceCap: 1 series dropped: an endpoint or a token's pushes bring at most {max}. | {n} series dropped: an endpoint or a token's pushes bring at most {max}.
dropped.orgCap: 1 new series refused: all {max} series of your plan are in use. A series is one line on a chart, not a call: the ones you already send keep flowing however often you send. | {n} new series refused: all {max} series of your plan are in use. A series is one line on a chart, not a call: the ones you already send keep flowing however often you send.
dropped.reserved: 1 series refused: names starting watchlog_ are WatchLog's own. | {n} series refused: names starting watchlog_ are WatchLog's own.
dropped.invalid: 1 series dropped: not a valid metric or label name. | {n} series dropped: not a valid metric or label name.

sources.removeBody: Its metrics stop arriving. What it sent stays until it ages out.

problem.gone: {metric} no longer reports. The widget shows it again when it does, or change the widget in Edit.
problem.refused: {metric} is refused: too many values for the label {label}. Nothing of it is stored.
problem.cluster: The cluster or fleet {metric} came from was deleted.

editor.noMetrics: This cluster or fleet reports no metric of its own yet. Add a source first.
editor.numberNoSplit: A number is one value: it isn't split.
editor.title: Title
editor.hint: Drag a widget by its handle to move it, by its corner to resize it. No queries: a widget is a metric, a shape and a size.

dashboards.limit: Your plan has one dashboard. | Your plan has {n} dashboards.
dashboards.name: Name
dashboards.emptyTitle: Build a dashboard from your metrics
dashboards.emptyBody: One widget at a time: pick a metric, how to show it, and its size. There is nothing to query and nothing to learn.
dashboards.noWidgets: This dashboard has no widget yet. Owners and Admins add them with Edit.
dashboards.widgetLimit: A dashboard has at most {n} widgets on your plan.
dashboards.drag: Move {name}: drag, or use the arrow keys
dashboards.corner: Resize {name}: drag, or use the arrow keys
dashboards.deleteBody: Its widgets go with it. The metrics stay.
dashboards.unsavedBody: The changes to this dashboard aren't saved yet.

watch.started: Watched: its usual range is learnt from now on (a week before it is used).
watch.pro: Watching a metric with What changed is part of Pro.

alerts.title: Alerts on your metrics
alerts.none: No alert on your metrics yet.
alerts.alsoUnder: These also appear with every other alert, and on the workload or server the metric belongs to, under
alerts.noChannels: No channel yet: add one under Settings.
alerts.watchFirst: Watch the metric with What changed first
alerts.name: Name (optional)
alerts.holdsNow: This holds right now: the alert would fire at once.
alerts.incomplete: Pick the metric and give the value.
alerts.deleteBody: It stops watching the metric. Alerts it raised resolve.
alerts.upgradeTitle: Alerts on your own metrics are part of Pro
alerts.upgradeBody: On Free you see your metrics, pin them and build a dashboard. Pro tells you when a number goes wrong: above or below a value, not reported, a backup too old, or outside its usual range.
